facts.title: Named for flint and stone
facts.text: The name silicon comes from the Latin words silex and silicis, meaning flint or hard stone, reflecting how common the element is in rocks. The English chemist Thomas Thomson coined the modern name in 1817, adding the -on ending to group it with the nonmetals carbon and boron. Earlier names like silicium are still used in many languages today, including French and German.

facts.title: First isolated in 1824
facts.text: Swedish chemist Jons Jacob Berzelius is credited with first isolating reasonably pure silicon in 1824 by heating potassium with silicon tetrafluoride and then washing away the byproducts. Humphry Davy and others had tried earlier and failed to get the pure element. Berzelius produced amorphous brown silicon; crystalline silicon was not made until Henri Sainte-Claire Deville did so in 1854.

facts.title: Earth's second most abundant element
facts.text: Silicon makes up about 28 percent of the Earth's crust by mass, making it the second most abundant element after oxygen. It is almost never found free in nature because it bonds so eagerly with oxygen to form silica and silicates. Quartz, sand, granite, clay, and mica are all built around silicon-oxygen frameworks.

facts.title: The brain of every computer
facts.text: Ultrapure silicon, refined to 99.9999999 percent purity (nine nines), is the foundation of nearly all modern electronics. As a semiconductor it can be precisely doped with traces of boron or phosphorus to control how it conducts electricity, which is the basis of the transistor. A single modern microchip can pack tens of billions of these silicon transistors into an area smaller than a fingernail.

facts.title: Why Silicon Valley got its name
facts.text: The nickname Silicon Valley was popularized by journalist Don Hoefler in a 1971 newspaper series about the chip industry south of San Francisco. The region became the heart of semiconductor manufacturing because companies there built integrated circuits from silicon wafers. The name has since become shorthand for the global technology industry itself.

facts.title: A diamond-like crystal
facts.text: Crystalline silicon shares the same tetrahedral diamond cubic structure as carbon diamond, with each atom bonded to four neighbors. It is a hard, brittle, blue-grey solid that shatters rather than bends, behaving like a ceramic. Unlike most metalloids it has a relatively high melting point of about 1,414 degrees Celsius.

facts.title: It expands when it freezes
facts.text: Like water, silicon is one of the few substances that is denser as a liquid than as a solid, so it expands when it solidifies. This unusual property comes from its open tetrahedral crystal structure, which takes up more room than the closely packed liquid. The same behavior is shared by germanium and gallium.

facts.title: Glass is mostly silicon dioxide
facts.text: Ordinary window glass is made primarily from silicon dioxide, the same compound found in quartz sand, melted with soda and lime. Pure fused silica can transmit ultraviolet light and withstand huge temperature swings, which is why it is used for laboratory glassware and telescope optics. The optical fibers carrying internet data across oceans are also drawn from ultrapure silica.

facts.title: Stardust forged silicate planets
facts.text: Silicon is produced inside massive stars through oxygen burning, and dying stars scatter it into space where it forms tiny silicate dust grains. These grains are the building blocks of rocky planets, which is why Earth, Mars, and the Moon are largely made of silicate minerals. Astronomers can detect this dust by the characteristic infrared light that silicate grains emit around young stars.

facts.title: Essential to life, but quietly
facts.text: Trace amounts of silicon play a structural role in living things, helping form connective tissue, bone, and skin in animals. Diatoms, a vast group of ocean microalgae, build intricate glass-like shells from dissolved silica and produce a large share of Earth's oxygen. In plants like rice and horsetail, silicon stiffens stems and helps defend against pests and disease.
